heading: Defining and Measuring AGI
takeaway: AGI is not a threshold you cross but a position on two continuous, independent axes — capability (task depth) and generality (domain breadth) — with autonomy layered on top as a separate, deployment-time choice rather than a property of the system itself.

ideas.label: consciousness/true-understanding is not required for an AI system to be dangerous; the safety-relevant question is capability, not consciousness
ideas.anchor: A system doesn't need to be conscious to cause harm.

misconceptions.claim: a system needs to be conscious or truly understand something to be dangerous
misconceptions.provenance: misreads the Chinese Room / consciousness discussion as implying an AI must 'truly understand' or be conscious to pose danger

misconceptions.claim: consciousness and intelligence are essentially the same axis
misconceptions.provenance: misreads 'consciousness often proves even harder to define than intelligence' as meaning the two are the same property rather than separable

ideas.label: safety-relevant definitions should be capability-focused (behaviorist): what a system can do, not how it got there or whether it is conscious, sets the risk profile
ideas.anchor: If a system can perform dangerous tasks whether through efficient learning or brute-force memorization, the risks exist either way.

misconceptions.claim: a system that learned inefficiently or via brute force is less dangerous than one that reached the same capability efficiently
misconceptions.provenance: misreads 'forget about internal mental states and focus on observable behavior' as meaning the learning path, not just the resulting capability, changes risk

misconceptions.claim: passing a conversational Turing-style test is sufficient evidence of general intelligence
misconceptions.provenance: misreads GPT-4 passing conversation tests as full validation of the behaviorist approach, ignoring the text's own correction that 'conversation is just one capability among many'

ideas.label: the adaptability/learning-efficiency view of intelligence (Chollet, Wang) prizes how efficiently a system acquires skills, not just final performance — but the text prioritizes final capability for safety purposes
ideas.anchor: the efficiency with which a system can turn experience and priors into skills

misconceptions.claim: learning efficiency and final capability are the same measure
misconceptions.provenance: misreads 'a system that needs a billion examples to learn what humans get from ten examples might be less impressive' as meaning sample-inefficient systems are less capable rather than merely less impressive by one criterion

misconceptions.claim: an AI that reached a capability through brute-force scale is inherently safer than one that learned it efficiently
misconceptions.provenance: misreads the adaptability view's emphasis on learning efficiency as implying safety risk tracks how a system learned rather than what it can now do

ideas.label: capability measures depth: how well a system executes one task, from 0% to superhuman — the first of two continuous axes replacing a binary AGI threshold
ideas.anchor: Capability measures depth - how good is the system at individual tasks.

misconceptions.claim: superhuman performance on one task means the system is broadly intelligent
misconceptions.provenance: misreads AlphaGo's superhuman Go performance as general intelligence rather than maximal depth on a single narrow task

misconceptions.claim: capability and generality are the same thing measured twice
misconceptions.provenance: misreads a system that is 'very good at one task' as thereby covering many domains, conflating depth with breadth

ideas.label: generality measures breadth: the percentage of cognitive domains where a system reaches expert-level capability, independent of how deep it goes on any one task
ideas.anchor: Generality is the percentage of these domains where a system achieves expert-level capability.

misconceptions.claim: generality just means very high performance
misconceptions.provenance: misreads generality as a measure of how good a system is rather than how many domains it covers, mirroring the depth/breadth conflation from the other direction

misconceptions.claim: generality requires superhuman performance in every domain
misconceptions.provenance: misreads 'expanding to more domains' as requiring maximal capability in each, rather than merely reaching the stated expert-level threshold in each

ideas.label: the framework is built to be continuous specifically to avoid binary AGI debates, yet the text still stipulates fixed AGI/TAI/ASI percentile thresholds for safety planning — a tension the reader must resolve, not a contradiction to dismiss
ideas.anchor: forcing everything into binary categories that lead to endless semantic debates about whether something "counts" as AGI

misconceptions.claim: since AGI is a continuum, terms like 'AGI' or 'ASI' are meaningless or never actually apply
misconceptions.provenance: misreads 'no universally agreed upon threshold where not-AGI suddenly becomes AGI' as meaning the framework refuses to give thresholds at all, missing that it then stipulates 80-90th percentile / 80-90% domain cutoffs anyway

misconceptions.claim: the AGI/TAI/ASI percentile thresholds contradict the chapter's continuous framework
misconceptions.provenance: misreads 'certain thresholds still matter for safety planning' as inconsistent with the continuum claim, rather than as thresholds layered on top of a continuous variable for practical use

ideas.label: AGI is defined by cognitive profile: matching a well-educated adult's versatility across most domains at expert level
ideas.anchor: Matching a well-educated adult's cognitive versatility and proficiency.

misconceptions.claim: AGI means superhuman performance at everything
misconceptions.provenance: misreads AGI's 'cognitive versatility' as requiring superhuman rather than merely expert-human (80-90th percentile) performance

misconceptions.claim: a system must be general in literally every domain to count as AGI
misconceptions.provenance: misreads 'AGI' / 'human-level AI (HLAI)' as needing near-total domain coverage rather than the stated 80-90% of domains

ideas.label: TAI is defined by impact potential, not cognitive architecture — a narrow-but-critical capability (e.g. automated ML R&D) can qualify as TAI without qualifying as AGI
ideas.anchor: TAI is defined by impact potential rather than cognitive architecture.

misconceptions.claim: TAI requires more capability or generality than AGI
misconceptions.provenance: misreads TAI as simply a higher-capability version of AGI rather than a differently-defined axis based on economic/social impact

misconceptions.claim: a narrow AI system cannot be transformative
misconceptions.provenance: misreads 'transformative AI' as needing broad cognitive versatility like AGI, missing that 'exceptional capability (99th percentile) on critical domains like automated ML R&D (20% of domains)' also counts as TAI

ideas.label: autonomy is a separate axis from capability/generality: it describes deployment (how much of a task the human vs. the AI does), and higher capability unlocks but does not require higher autonomy
ideas.anchor: For safety purposes, capability and deployment autonomy should be considered separately.

misconceptions.claim: more capable AI is automatically more autonomous
misconceptions.provenance: misreads a highly capable AI system as inherently more autonomous or agentic, when the text states autonomy is a deployment choice independent of capability

misconceptions.claim: if a system is capable enough for Level 5 autonomy, it should be deployed at Level 5
misconceptions.provenance: misreads 'higher capability levels unlock higher autonomy' as capability requiring or mandating high autonomy, rather than merely making it possible while lower autonomy remains available

misconceptions.claim: a system deployed at a higher autonomy level is inherently more dangerous than the same system at a lower level
misconceptions.provenance: conflates autonomy level with danger level directly, missing that 'autonomy level affects risk exposure, not inherent danger'

ideas.label: percentage/threshold-based AGI scores can mislead: they can imply linear progress toward AGI when remaining capabilities are disproportionately hard, and human psychometric batteries (CHC) may miss capabilities universal in humans but absent in AI
ideas.anchor: human psychometric taxonomies like CHC may miss capabilities universal in humans but lacking in AI

misconceptions.claim: each additional percentage point of an 'AGI score' represents an equally-sized step toward AGI
misconceptions.provenance: misreads a rising percentage AGI score as meaning progress toward AGI is roughly linear, when 'final capabilities may represent disproportionately difficult bottlenecks'

misconceptions.claim: matching a human's percentile score on a test means matching human-level competence on that construct
misconceptions.provenance: misreads an LLM scoring 90% on a human psychometric test (e.g. Raven's progressive matrices) as comparable to a human scoring 90%, per 'An LLM scoring 90% on a Raven's progressive matrices test is not comparable to a human scoring 90%'

ideas.label: the (t,n)-AGI framework defines AGI via time-and-scale (matching n experts working for time t) rather than percentile-domain coverage, and explicitly does not credit running many copies of an AI in parallel
ideas.anchor: AGI can also be defined through a combination of time and scale

misconceptions.claim: a (one year, eight billion)-AGI could be achieved by running one AI many times in parallel rather than genuinely matching sustained expert-level performance
misconceptions.provenance: misreads the (t,n)-AGI framework as accounting for parallel copies, when the text states it 'does not account for how many copies of the AI run simultaneously'

misconceptions.claim: a one-year AGI must sustain a single unbroken task for a full year
misconceptions.provenance: misreads 'one-year AGI would beat humans at basically everything' as requiring continuous unbroken work, missing that 'most projects can be divided into sub-tasks that can be completed in shorter timeframes'

ideas.label: the ten CHC cognitive domains as an enumerated list
ideas.anchor: These break down into ten core capabilities from the Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory
ideas.reason: enumeration; L2 at best; the domains are scaffolding for DM-5, not an idea in themselves

ideas.label: the six autonomy levels (0-5) as an enumerated list
ideas.anchor: Level 0: No AI - Pure human operation.
ideas.reason: enumeration; DM-9 already tests the concept that matters (autonomy is separable from capability), the specific level list is recall

ideas.label: Legg & Hutter's goal-achievement definition of intelligence
ideas.anchor: Intelligence measures an agent's ability to achieve goals in a wide range of environments
ideas.reason: text explicitly discards it as 'too abstract for practical measurement'; best used as a family-d right-idea-wrong-slot distractor for DM-2/DM-4 questions, not its own idea

ideas.label: OpenAI's and Anthropic's capability-based public definitions of AGI/TAI
ideas.anchor: highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work
ideas.reason: illustrative company definitions the text itself calls 'too vague... lack precision'; colour for DM-2/DM-8, not independently testable

discrimination_pairs.conflation: readers think a system's risk depends on whether it reached a capability through efficient learning versus brute-force scale, rather than on the resulting capability itself (the destination, not the path)
readers merge capability (how good at one task) with generality (how many domains), e.g. reading AlphaGo's superhuman narrow performance as evidence of broad/general intelligence

readers treat AGI and TAI as the same milestone at different sizes, missing that TAI is defined by impact potential and can be reached via narrow-but-critical capability rather than broad cognitive versatility
readers treat a highly capable/general system as automatically highly autonomous, merging what a system can do with how independently it is deployed
